Vignette: Maya, Age 38

Maya has worked behind the bar at the same neighborhood pub for nearly a decade. She knows her regulars by name, knows their drinks before they sit down, and has always prided herself on being the kind of person who stays steady when things get loud. She is quick with a joke, quicker with a pour, and the kind of woman who holds the room together without anyone noticing she is doing it. That steadiness, she says, is something she learned long before she ever picked up a cocktail shaker.

Fourteen months ago, Maya's younger brother Darius was struck by a car while crossing an intersection two blocks from her apartment. She was not there when it happened. She got the call on a Tuesday evening mid-shift, and she remembers the exact song that was playing on the bar speakers when her phone lit up with her mother's number. She drove to the hospital still wearing her apron. Darius survived, but he spent three weeks in the ICU with a traumatic brain injury and underwent two surgeries. For the first ten days, the doctors were not sure he would make it. Maya sat in the waiting room every night after her shifts ended, sometimes still smelling like beer and citrus, watching the clock move in a way that felt mechanical and wrong.

Darius recovered enough to go home, though he continues to struggle with memory and fatigue. Most people in Maya's life consider the story to have a happy ending. Maya does not feel that way, though she has difficulty explaining why, even to herself.

She still sees it — not the accident, which she did not witness, but the version her mind constructed from the details she was given: the intersection, the headlights, Darius's body. The image arrives without warning. It comes when she is slicing limes, when she is lying in bed next to her partner, when she is driving and passes a crosswalk. Her chest tightens and for a moment she is certain, on some wordless level, that he is already gone.

She avoids the street where it happened. She has reorganized her entire commute around not passing that intersection, adding seven minutes to a drive she has made thousands of times. She has also stopped answering her phone during shifts unless she recognizes the number, because unknown calls now carry a weight they never used to.

Sleep is difficult. She lies awake rehearsing conversations she had with Darius before the accident, wondering whether she was a good enough sister, whether she called him enough, whether she told him things that mattered. Her partner, a patient man named Theo, has noticed that she flinches when he touches her unexpectedly and that she has become quieter in a way that is different from simply being tired. She knows he has noticed. She has not found a way to talk to him about it.

At the bar, she is still good at her job. She can still read a room, still manage a difficult customer, still make a stranger feel welcome. But there are moments — when someone comes in shaken, when she overhears a phone call that sounds urgent, when an ambulance passes the window — that she has to step into the back cooler for a minute and press her hands against the cold metal shelving until the feeling passes. She tells herself she is fine because Darius is alive. She tells herself that what she went through is not the kind of thing that counts.

But she cries on the drive home more nights than not, and she has started declining invitations to family dinners because sitting across from her brother and watching him search for words he cannot find is something she has not yet learned how to bear.
